outcomes.text: Describe the Versailles Peace Settlement and what it imposed.
Explain the work and successes of the League of Nations in the 1920s.
Describe the international agreements of the 1920s: Dawes Plan, Locarno, Kellogg-Briand, Young Plan.
Describe attempts at disarmament.
Explain the impact of the worldwide economic depression on international relations.
Explain how tension grew in Europe in the 1930s and why the League of Nations failed.
Explain the policy of appeasement and the outbreak of war in 1939.
Describe the actions of the USSR in Eastern Europe 1945-1948 and the response of the USA and its allies.
Explain the roles of the Yalta and Potsdam conferences.
Describe the division of Germany, the Truman Doctrine and the Marshall Plan.
Explain the Berlin Blockade and Airlift.
Describe the development of NATO and the Warsaw Pact.
Explain the building of the Berlin Wall in 1961 and its effects on international relations.
Explain the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962.
Describe the origins of US involvement in Vietnam 1954-65.
Explain US tactics in the Vietnam War and their consequences.
Explain Vietcong tactics and their consequences.
Explain US withdrawal from Vietnam, including opposition in the USA.
Explain the end of the war and its impact on international relations.
Explain how the Second World War, the Cold War and new evidence since about 1990 led to differing interpretations of appeasement.
Explain how the internal culture and politics of the USSR and USA, the Vietnam War and new evidence since about 1990 led to differing interpretations of responsibility for the Cold War.

topics.title: Key issues for all depth studies

subtopics.title: Key issues of the people and the state

outcomes.text: Explain the policies of the state, including their aims and how they were implemented.
Explain the impact of the state on different groups: social classes, women, young people, religious and ethnic groups.
Explain the reasons for, and extent of, support or opposition to the state from different groups.
Use source material from the time to investigate these issues and recognise the challenges of primary sources.
Describe early purges against opposition in cities, countryside and regions in the 1950s.
Explain the intentions and impact of the Hundred Flowers campaign.
Explain Communist social policies under Mao and how they differed from Chinese traditionalism.
Describe policies towards women, young people and education.
Explain agricultural policies including land reform, collectivisation and their impact.
Explain industrial policy including the First Five Year Plan.
Explain the Great Leap Forward, its effect across society and why it failed.
Use Dazhai Commune as a case study of Mao's economic policies.
Explain the reasons for the Cultural Revolution.
Explain its impact on the people, including intellectuals and students.
Describe the role of the Red Guards.
Describe the impact of Communism in Tibet.
Explain Communist propaganda and its impact, including Mao's personality cult.
Use Dazhai as a case study of Communist Party repression.
Explain attitudes to opposition and repression after 1976, including the Gang of Four and the democracy wall.
Explain changes in economic policy under Deng, including the Four Modernisations, and their impact.
Explain Communist propaganda in this period and its impact.
Explain social changes under Deng: role of women, education changes and the One Child policy.

topics.title: Rise and consolidation of the Nazi regime 1925-1934

subtopics.title: Weimar and the rise of the Nazis

outcomes.text: Assess the strengths and weaknesses of the Weimar Republic 1925-1928.
Describe Nazi policies in the 1920s and the party's position in 1928.
Explain the impact of the Depression on different groups in Germany.
Explain the political, social and economic crisis of 1929-1933 and rising Nazi support.
Explain the Reichstag Fire, the suspension of the Weimar constitution and the Enabling Act.
Explain the March 1933 elections.
Explain the takeover of, or collaboration with, key institutions, particularly the army.
Explain the elimination of opposition: trade unions, opposition parties and the SA.
Describe the Nazi terror state: SA, SS, Gestapo, SD, courts and police.
Explain Nazi use of culture and propaganda.
Explain Hitler's personal popularity.
Explain attempts to create a National Community.
Explain why there was no effective opposition.
Explain Nazi economic policies and their effects on winners and losers.
Explain Nazi social policies, including those on women and youth.
Describe persecution of Jews and other groups: Roma, Jehovah's Witnesses and homosexuals.
Describe eugenics policies.
Describe the initial reaction to the outbreak of war and Germany's changing fortunes, including colonisation in the East.
Explain the growing impact of war, including bombing, and the extent of support for the war effort.
Describe opposition during the war.
Explain the escalation of racial persecution leading to the Holocaust.
Describe defeat and occupation.
Explain Allied de-Nazification, its methods and impact.
Compare the experiences of people in East and West Germany 1945-1955.

topics.title: Opposition to the Apartheid regime c.1960s

outcomes.text: Explain the consolidation of Apartheid: Separate Development and the Bantustans.
Explain the nature and extent of support for Apartheid and the methods used to maintain it.
Explain the Sharpeville Massacre and its impact.
Explain the reasons for, methods of and impact of resistance: ANC, Freedom Charter, Umkhonto we Sizwe and Poqo.
Explain the Rivonia Trial of 1964 and its consequences.
Describe the Black Consciousness Movement, SASO, women's groups and trade unions, including the 1973 Durban strike.
Explain the Soweto students' uprising of 1976.
Describe the ANC in exile and the international Anti-Apartheid Movement.
Explain the impact of resistance on the regime and the regime's response.
Explain growing pressure on the regime: sanctions, the United Democratic Front and mass resistance.
Explain the growth of Inkatha, civil war and its impact on Black communities.
Explain opposition to the 1983 constitution and the State of Emergency 1985-1990.
Explain divisions in the National Party and the failure of total strategy, including Cuito Cuanavale.
Describe the roles of FW de Klerk, Ramaphosa and Mandela.
Explain negotiations between the government and the ANC.
Explain the unbanning of the ANC, PAC and South African Communist Party.
Describe the first free elections in 1994.
Explain the US economy in the 1920s including Republican policies and ideology.
Identify industries and social groups that did and did not prosper.
Explain the US government and women in the 1920s, including women's rights movements and the Sheppard-Towner Act.
Explain the causes, aims, implementation and failure of prohibition.
Explain prejudice and discrimination in US society, including Jim Crow laws and the Ku Klux Klan.
Explain the Red Scare, the Palmer Raids and Sacco and Vanzetti.
Describe immigration restrictions through the 1920s.
Describe attempts to combat prejudice, including the NAACP and the UNIA.

subtopics.title: Depression and the first New Deal

outcomes.text: Explain the economic and social effects of the Great Depression and the government response.
Describe the 1932 presidential election campaigns.
Explain the First New Deal: the Hundred Days and Alphabet Agencies (AAA, CCC, FERA, NRA, TVA).
Explain the Second New Deal: WPA, Social Security Act, Wagner Act, Resettlement Administration and Farm Security Administration.
Assess reactions to, and the impact of, the New Deals.

topics.title: The impact of the Second World War on US society

outcomes.text: Explain mobilisation for the war effort: propaganda campaigns, war production and the end of the Depression.
Explain increased government and presidential powers, including control of wages and prices.
Describe the population's response to US involvement in the war.
Describe the social impact: rationing, tax on luxuries, housing shortages and rising divorce.
Explain the role of women in the war effort and Japanese internment.
Explain the war as foundation for the Civil Rights movement: Detroit Race Riots 1943, segregation in the military, Executive Order 8802 and desegregation in 1948.
Explain US government concerns about Communist influence and responses, including media campaigns promoting American values.
Explain the Red Scare of the late 1940s, J Edgar Hoover and the Rosenberg case, and reactions to it.
Explain the nature of, support for and opposition to McCarthyism.
Describe the position of African Americans: Jim Crow laws, access to education, voting rights and unequal employment.
Describe the development and achievements of the movement, including Brown vs. Board of Education 1954 and the Montgomery Bus Boycott 1956.
Explain the leadership of Martin Luther King in civil rights campaigns.
Explain the roles of SNCC, SCLC and NAACP in campaigns.
Explain opposition to the movement, including illegal organisations, police and state authorities.
Explain the contribution of government and official institutions, including the Supreme Court.
Explain the roles of Kennedy and Johnson in civil rights campaigns.
Explain the reasons for, and impact of, the Civil Rights Act 1964.
Explain the development and impact of African American radical movements and leaders, including Malcolm X and Black Power.
Explain the impact of civil rights campaigns for Native Americans and Chicanos.
Explain the development of feminist movements, including Betty Friedan and NOW.
Explain the impact of feminism: Status Commission 1963, Equal Pay Act, use of the Civil Rights Act and the 1972 Supreme Court ruling.
Describe the Stonewall riots of 1969.
Explain political, economic and social divisions in the USA, including anti-Vietnam War protests.
Explain campaigns to improve the welfare of the poor, Johnson's Great Society and Nixon's welfare pledges.

topics.title: Change and continuity across long periods

outcomes.text: Identify and outline key features of each section of a thematic study.
Explain key themes and developments in each section, with causes and effects and how causes connect.
Show understanding of change: its causes, consequences, nature, rate and extent, and of continuity.
Explain the significance of the developments studied.
Use concepts of cause, consequence, change, continuity and significance to compare sections within and across eras.

units.title: Thematic study: Migration to Britain c.1000-c.2010

outcomes.text: Explain differing political, economic, social and religious reasons for immigration.
Describe the experience and actions of immigrants, including community contribution and resistance to discrimination.
Describe responses to immigration from government and established communities.
Explain the social, cultural, economic, religious and political impact of immigration.
Explain the impact of immigration on Britain's relationship with the wider world.
Explain how ideas of Englishness and Britishness have been defined from c.1500.
Describe population diversity in England before 1066, the Norman Conquest and resistance to the Normans.
Explain the arrival of Jews in 1066, their treatment until expulsion in 1290.
Describe resident aliens in medieval England, their treatment and integration.

subtopics.title: Migration in the early modern period

outcomes.text: Explain why Africans came to sixteenth century England and their experiences.
Describe the East India Company and arrivals from the Indian subcontinent: Lascars, child servants and ayahs.
Explain the growth of African communities: Royal African Company, enslaved trade, loss of American colonies and empire expansion.
Describe the readmission of Jews in 1656 and Protestant refugees such as Huguenots and Palatines, including their reception and assimilation.
Explain the impact of the Industrial Revolution on migration, including Irish and Scottish migrants.
Explain the impact of migrants on the Abolition movement and the Chartists.
Describe Eastern European Jewish immigrants, their experiences and impact.
Explain naturalisation and denization and legislation such as the Naturalisation Act 1870.
Describe the growth of diverse port communities in the early twentieth century.
Explain the reasons for and impact of the Aliens Act 1905, Status of Aliens Act 1914 and British Nationality Act 1948.
Describe the arrival of Jewish refugees in the 1930s and attitudes to them.
Describe migrants' experiences in the two world wars and the Poles who settled after the Second World War.
Explain the reasons for Commonwealth migration after the Second World War and immigrants' experiences and impact.
Explain the resulting debate: political racism, antiracism, race relations law and the 1962 and 1981 Acts.
Explain immigration as a political issue c.1990-c.2010: multi-cultural society debate, asylum seekers and EU open borders.

units.title: Thematic study: Power: Monarchy and Democracy in Britain c.1000-2014

outcomes.text: Identify individuals, institutions and groups with power: monarchs, aristocracy, gentry, elected representatives, and the social structures dividing elites from the ruled.
Explain claims to power: religious, legal, hereditary, democratic principles and force.
Explain methods of maintaining power: military force, religion, propaganda, ideas, institutions, negotiation and compromise.
Explain challenges to power and power changing hands: religion, ideology, ambition, uprisings and elite power struggles.

subtopics.title: Kingship and the struggle for power

outcomes.text: Explain Anglo-Saxon kingship c.1000-1066: its basis, the kings' powers and responsibilities, and relations with thegns.
Explain the competing claims to the throne in 1066 and the Norman Conquest's transfer of power at all levels of society.
Assess the power of the monarch and barons by 1087.
Describe John's accession, early revolts against his rule and Magna Carta.
Explain the emergence of Parliament under Henry III and Edward I, including Simon de Montfort.
Explain the deposition of Richard II in 1399 and the Wars of the Roses.

subtopics.title: Tudor government and the Stuart crisis

outcomes.text: Explain the growth of royal power under Henry VIII and the role of Parliament under Henry VIII and Elizabeth I.
Explain Charles I's personal rule 1629-1640, the Civil Wars, the abolition of the monarchy and the Restoration in 1660.
Explain James II's rule and the reasons for the 1688 Glorious Revolution.
Explain the legacy of the Glorious Revolution, including the Bill of Rights.
Explain the development of Parliament under William III and Anne and the emergence of political parties and a parliamentary monarchy.
Explain dissatisfaction with the electoral system by the early 1800s.
Explain the reasons for and impact of the Reform Acts of 1832, 1867 and 1884.
Explain the rise and effectiveness of mass Trade Unions and the Labour Party 1880s-1914.
Explain the struggle for the vote for women and why some won it in 1918.
Explain government control in the world wars and the increased role of the state from 1945 to c.1980.
Explain challenges to Parliament c.1980 to early 2000s: Miners' Strike 1984-1985, CND and Greenpeace.
Explain Prime Ministerial power under Thatcher and Blair, devolution and the challenges of coalition government.

units.title: Thematic study: War and British Society c.790-c.2010

outcomes.text: Compare the impacts of different types of war: defence, conquest, religion and civil war.
Explain attitudes and responses to war among civilians and military personnel.
Explain the impacts of war on people, military and civilian.
Explain the impacts of war on the relationship between governments and people.
Explain the impact of, and responses to, Viking raids on Anglo-Saxon England 790-1066.
Explain English resistance to the Norman Conquest and Norman control under William I.
Explain the feudal system and the extent of the Normans' impact on different levels of society.
Explain the feudal relationship between monarchs and barons and its breakdown under Stephen 1135-1154 and John 1214-1216.
Explain the changing nature of war c.1290-c.1450 and the adaptation of feudal service.
Explain the financial cost of war and its impact on populations where armies fought or were stationed.
Explain Elizabeth I's wars with Spain and their impact on the monarch's prestige and relations with Parliament.
Explain the actions of English privateers and their impact on security, economy and people.
Explain warfare on the English-Scottish borders c.1500-c.1600 and its impact on border society.
Explain the nature of the Civil Wars of 1642-1651 and their impact on England, Scotland and Ireland.
Explain the Jacobite Wars of 1715 and 1745 and the repression of the Jacobites in Scotland.
Explain gains from the Seven Years War 1756-1763 and their effects on Britain.
Explain the wars against Revolutionary and Napoleonic France and their effects on British society and politics.
Explain the effects of the Crimean War and the Boer Wars of 1880-1881 and 1899-1902.
Explain the beginnings of total war in the First and Second World Wars, increased state power and the changing state-people relationship.
Explain the Cold War and Britain in the 1950s and 1960s and IRA campaigns 1969-1994.
Explain the Iraq War of 2003 and terrorist threats and counter measures after 2003.

units.title: Depth study: The Impact of Empire on Britain 1688-c.1730

topics.title: English expansion and its impact on the British Isles c.1688-c.1730

outcomes.text: Explain the significance of the Glorious Revolution and Hanoverian succession for England's position, including campaigns in Ireland 1688-1691.
Explain England-Scotland relations after 1688: Jacobite opposition, Glencoe 1692, the Darien Scheme and Act of Union 1707.
Describe the Jacobite Rebellion of 1715 and emigration, including forced emigration, to the Americas.

topics.title: Economic impact of empire on Britain 1688-c.1730

outcomes.text: Explain the economic impact of war and imperial expansion, including the Bank of England 1694.
Explain growing trade with India and China, Kolkata and the East India Company.
Explain the lifting of the Royal African Company monopoly 1698, the Treaty of Utrecht 1713 and the South Sea Bubble 1719.
Explain the importance of North American and Caribbean colonies and the origins of the slave-based economy.

topics.title: Political and social impact of empire on Britain 1688-c.1730

outcomes.text: Explain the emergence of consumerism and its political and economic impact.
Describe British involvement in the slave trade: Bristol, Liverpool, London and smaller ports.
Explain the growth of ideas of racial hierarchy and their impact on minority communities.
Explain opposition to slavery, including slave resistance, and the role of coffee houses in political activism.

units.title: Depth study: The English Reformation c.1520-c.1550

subtopics.title: The Church and calls for reform

outcomes.text: Explain the role, importance and wealth of the church in England c.1520.
Describe religious practice and the relationship between church and ordinary people.
Explain the role and impact of Lollard and Luther's ideas, critics of the church in the 1530s and popular attitudes to reform.
Explain Henry VIII's desire to annul his first marriage and the Reformation Parliament's legislation 1529-1534.
Describe Thomas Cromwell, the Valor Ecclesiasticus and the Visitation of the Monasteries.
Explain the process of dissolution and the Suppression Acts of 1536 and 1539.
Explain immediate reactions: support, opportunism and opposition.
Explain effects on religious orders and on ordinary people, especially the old and poor.
Describe cultural impacts of dissolution.
Explain resistance and protest, including the Lincolnshire Rising and the Pilgrimage of Grace 1536-1537.

topics.title: The impact of the Reformation in English parishes c.1534-c.1550

outcomes.text: Explain developments in religious policy under Henry VIII and Edward VI.
Explain effects on worship: services, prayer books and the English Bible.
Explain the impact on church buildings and the clergy.
Explain enforcement of new policies, ordinary people's responses and resistance such as the Prayer Book Rebellion 1549.

units.title: Depth study: Personal Rule to Restoration 1629-1660

topics.title: Relationship between Parliament and Charles I 1629-1642

outcomes.text: Explain why Charles I called Parliament in 1640.
Explain the Long Parliament's criticisms of the Personal Rule: financial and religious measures and suppression of criticism.
Explain attacks on Laud and Strafford.
Explain events leading to civil war: Irish rebellion 1641, Grand Remonstrance, attempt on the Five Members, Militia Ordinance and Nineteen Propositions.
Explain divisions within Parliament 1640-1642.

topics.title: The political and religious impact of war 1642-1649

outcomes.text: Explain Parliament's attempts to reach agreement with Charles I 1646-1647, including the Propositions of Newcastle.
Explain Parliament's reaction to new groups: Levellers, Quakers and Diggers.
Explain the relationship between Parliament and the Army, Presbyterians and Independents, and the debate about settlement.
Explain the execution of Charles I in 1649, the Rump Parliament and the declaration of the Republic.

topics.title: The nature and extent of political and religious change 1649-c.1660

outcomes.text: Explain the relationship between the Rump Parliament and Cromwell 1649-1653.
Explain Parliament's relationship with Cromwell 1653-1658, including the Instrument of Government and the Major Generals.
Explain the Humble Petition and Advice and Cromwell's response.
Explain attempts to reach a settlement September 1658 to April 1660 and the terms of the Restoration.

units.title: Study of the historic environment: Urban Environments: Patterns of Migration

outcomes.text: Explain how historians use the physical fabric of the site and related documents to understand changing patterns of migration.
Analyse and evaluate physical and documentary sources: buildings, names and signs, monuments, on-site information, maps, oral histories and local collections.
Investigate how the site is presented, what is absent and what further research is needed.

subtopics.title: Arrival and reception in the site

outcomes.text: Describe the history of immigration to and emigration from the area, where people came from and why.
Explain how patterns of migration changed and how this shows in the urban environment.
Explain how and where groups settled and positive and negative responses from the receiving population and authorities.

subtopics.title: Life, events and impact in the site

outcomes.text: Describe immigrants' housing, welfare, living conditions, employment, faith and community organisations.
Describe key events in local migration history, where they happened and how they are commemorated.
Explain the economic, social, political and cultural impact of migration and the current multicultural community.

units.title: Study of the historic environment: Castles: Form and Function c.1000-1750

outcomes.text: Explain the strategic, geographical and physical location of Kenilworth Castle.
Describe key features such as motte and bailey layouts, stone towers, defences, great hall and causeway.
Explain when and why features were installed or removed, including slighting, and what this shows about the country at the time.
Describe the evidence historians use: maps, drawings, contracts, plans and aerial photographs.

subtopics.title: Using and living in the castle

outcomes.text: Explain Kenilworth as a means of conquest, baronial and royal power, administration, justice and a dwelling.
Describe lives of castle owners such as the De Clintons, de Montfort, John of Gaunt, Tudors, Dudleys, Stuarts and Hydes.
Describe the people who made the castle function, such as blacksmiths and cooks.
Describe the evidence used: royal licences, newspaper articles, bills, accounts and inventories.
Connect Kenilworth to events including baronial and other rebellions, border warfare and civil war sieges.
Explain how castles in general served as military bases, centres of power, residences and administrative centres, and how their purpose changed.
